Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Dr. Alejandro Reyes was forty years old, a trauma surgeon at a busy metropolitan hospital, when the wildfire that had been moving through the foothills for days suddenly crested the ridge behind his neighborhood. He had been home that evening, his wife Sofia already at work, and the evacuation order came too late for him to do more than grab a duffel bag and his dog. The noise was the first thing that stayed with him—the roar of the flames, the sharp crack of trees exploding, the distant popping of gas lines. For the next two hours he drove through smoke so thick that his headlights seemed useless, the acrid smell seeping into the car, into his clothes, into his lungs. He later learned that his house was gone, and that an elderly neighbor had not made it out. At the hospital the next morning, still reeking of smoke, he scrubbed in for an emergency case and tried to push the images away. He could not.

In the months that followed, Alejandro found that certain sounds would send him back to that night without warning. A cart clattering in the hallway, the heavy slam of a trauma room door, the clang of metal trays—each could drop him into the heat and the panic, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. He had come to believe that these intrusions were a sign that he was broken, that he had not done enough, that he should have saved the neighbor or been faster or calmer. He tried not to think about it, but the memory was incomplete—fragments of flame, the texture of smoke, the feel of the steering wheel, but whole stretches of that evening missing. When he did recall what he could, what filled him was not fear but immense, crushing grief. He would find himself tearing up in the scrub room, overwhelmed by a sadness that had no clear object, just the weight of all that was lost.

At first, Alejandro coped by working longer hours. Surgery demanded his full attention, and the focus was a relief. He would volunteer for the most complex cases, staying at the hospital until late, then come home and pour himself a whiskey—or two, or three—to numb the edge. On nights when the images surfaced despite the alcohol, he would turn to sex with Sofia, not out of desire but out of urgency, using the physical intensity to drown out the intrusive memories. He had come to rely on this pattern: distraction by work, chemical dampening by drink, then a frantic sexual release that left him hollow. His wife had begun to notice his distance, his irritability, the way he avoided talking about the fire or anything that reminded him of it. She had confronted him gently, but he had brushed her off, certain that if he stopped managing the memories they would consume him entirely.

The hospital itself had become a landscape of triggers. The smell of burnt coffee in the break room could make him queasy. A fire alarm drill sent him into a cold sweat, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom. He began taking the stairs instead of the elevator, worried that a sudden jolt or noise would cause him to freeze in front of colleagues. He had not fully avoided any procedure, but he had started planning his movements more carefully, scanning his environment for anything that might set him off. The vigilance was exhausting, and he knew his concentration was slipping. A month ago, during a routine laparoscopic case, the anesthesia machine beeped loudly and he flinched, his hands trembling for a moment. No one said anything, but he saw the scrub nurse look at him oddly.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the near miss in surgery, but his wife’s quiet admission that she had moved into the guest room three nights ago. She had told him she could not keep living with a man who was only half-present, who drank himself to sleep and used her body as a medication. Alejandro had sat in the kitchen afterward, the smell of burnt toast from that morning hitting him sideways, and the full memory of the fire—what little he had—flashed again, along with a grief so profound he sank to the floor. He called the employee assistance program the next day. What he hoped for was to stop the intrusions, to be able to walk through the hospital without bracing for impact. What he feared was that he had already lost his home once, and that this time he would lose the only person who had stayed.
